newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CSU says won't relent on hard euro criteria.
newsitem.headline: German CSU says won't relent on hard euro criteria.

text.p: A dispute within Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition over how strictly to interpret rules to qualify for a European single currency deepened on Monday with the Christian Social Union (CSU) insisting that Germany fulfil membership criteria exactly.
Bernd Protzner, secretary general of the CSU which is the Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), made the CSU's views clear in an interview with the Rheinische Post newspaper.
Despite withering criticism from Kohl, who blasted Bavaria's CSU premier Edmund Stoiber for "unusually foolish talk" on the euro currency criteria, Protzner said the CSU stood fully behind Stoiber.

"The chancellor does not have the right to give directives to the Bavarian premier," Protzner said. "The CSU has said clearly and unanimously that it will not allow the single European currency to be born with a birth defect."
Protzner said it was still more important to meet the stability criteria than the 1999 timetable for the euro's launch. The CSU would not relent on the issue, he said.

The unusual row between the CSU and Kohl, whose coalition also includes the centrist Free Democrats, flared publicly in recent days when the chancellor issued warnings to intermediaries for Stoiber that he should stop insisting on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.
The dispute between Kohl, a strong advocate of the euro, and Stoiber is ostensibly about how strictly to assess the finances of states wanting to launch Europe's single currency.

But some German media commentators have observed that, with two-thirds of the population opposed to the euro replacing their deutschemarks, Stoiber's insistence on a strict interpretation of the treaty could be seen as an elegant way to thwart the project so few Germans want.

European Union states wanting to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) must post a maximum budget deficit of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) as set down in the Maastricht Treaty on EMU.
To Kohl's irritation, Stoiber has been insisting with increasing vigour that the project should be delayed if the target is even fractionally missed.

Kohl's powerful lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble told MDR radio on Sunday he was confident Germany would pass the financial test to qualify for launching Europe's planned single currency, the euro, in 1999 and argued three percent did not have to mean 3.0.
"Germany will fulfil the criteria to qualify for the euro. The figures after the decimal point are important but not decisive," Schaueble, CDU/CSU parliamentary group leader.
"The essential thing is to set the course for undoubted lasting stability of the European currency," he said.
Kohl, speaking at a Group of Seven (G7) summit in Denver, stood on his insistence that the euro would arrive on time. But he omitted to say how strictly it would fulfil the criteria.
"I have never doubted this...My (G7) colleagues are in absolutely no doubt about this," Kohl told German television.
Bavarian finance minister Erwin Huber said EMU should not go ahead unless participants strictly met the Maastricht criteria. This, Huber said, was a chief guarantee of stability for the planned euro.

German newspapers reported that Kohl had criticised the CSU in Bavaria during last week's European Union summit in Amsterdam for their "unusally foolish talk" of keeping to the 3.0 interpretation of the criteria.
Stoiber said on Sunday Kohl had criticised another leading CSU figure there on the edge of the EU summit, Kurt Faltlhauser, for brewing trouble for EMU.

Stoiber said he failed to comprehend such criticism because Kohl's CDU relied on the CSU for its 12-seat majority in the Bundestag lower house of parliament in Bonn and would not be in power without the Bavarian party.
